tagline: Compare methods for choosing actions and estimating their returns in simulations of intensive care.
intro: EHRDyn is a benchmark for offline reinforcement learning, which learns a policy for choosing actions from previously recorded data, using electronic health records (EHRs) from intensive care units. This leaderboard shows aggregate paper results for 21 policy specifications and six methods for estimating policy returns. Policies are evaluated by running them in simulators fitted to the MIMIC-IV database and in controlled synthetic environments, so returns describe simulation outcomes rather than clinical treatment benefits.
how_to_read: Return measures the reward accumulated by a policy. Control-scaled return sets the worst of four fixed reference policies, called controls, to 0 and the best to 1 within each task or environment. A value above 1 beats that task's or environment's best control.
Mean returns give equal weight to each of the five fitted tasks or five controlled profiles. A profile groups the synthetic environments for one task.

The best single control is the fixed control with the highest mean across tasks or profiles. It is the behavior policy in the fitted simulators and minimum action in the controlled environments. It can differ from the best control for an individual task.

The 95% interval describes uncertainty in the difference from the best single control. Fitted intervals account only for Monte Carlo sampling uncertainty over five fixed tasks. Controlled intervals use bootstrap resampling of environments within each profile.
An interval that includes zero does not distinguish the method from the best single control. An interval entirely above zero supports a higher return in that simulator family.
policies_note_fitted: No method has a 95% interval entirely above zero for its difference from the behavior policy, the best single control. The method listed as HGB residual + planner has the largest estimated gain, +0.102, with a 95% interval from -0.049 to +0.252.
policies_note_controlled: All seven methods that pair a transition model, which predicts the next state, with a planner, which uses those predictions to choose actions, have 95% intervals entirely above zero, with estimated gains from +0.068 to +0.100 over minimum action. These include the persistence planner, which predicts no state change, so the gains cannot be attributed to learned dynamics.
chart_axis_label: Difference from the best single control in control-scaled return
tasks_above_note: The column counts how many of the five fitted tasks have a method beating that task's best control with a standardized difference z above 2.
per_task_note: Compare each method's control-scaled return for sepsis, respiratory support, shock, acute kidney injury (AKI), and heart-failure (HF) decongestion. The fitted view shows one result per task, and the controlled view shows the average across the eight environments in each task profile.
ope_note: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates a policy's return from data collected by another policy, and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) measures average absolute estimation error relative to the range of returns across the four controls in fitted simulators or the feasible range of returns in controlled environments. Cov90 is the fraction of nominal 90% intervals that contain the reference return, Spearman is the rank correlation between estimated and reference returns, and pairwise ordering is the fraction of policy pairs ordered correctly, with 0.5 representing chance. No estimator is jointly best at error, interval coverage, and policy ordering.
caveats: The EHR data come from one database, MIMIC-IV.
There is no sealed test set of real EHRs.
Results describe named implementations run with fixed budgets. They do not compare algorithms using matched amounts of computation.
Comparisons in the fitted simulators depend on the weights those simulators use to update the state.
The results do not establish a single exact ranking of methods.
about_text: EHRDyn version 2.2.0 is released under the MIT license at https://github.com/cys1102/ehrdyn. The EHR-fitted family uses one frozen simulator per task, fitted to MIMIC-IV, and its returns are implied by those models rather than measured clinical policy values. Building these simulators requires credentialed MIMIC-IV access. The controlled family contains 40 public synthetic environments, with eight variants for each of five task profiles, whose specified rules make true returns known.
submit_text: Submissions are not possible today: no submission system exists. Controlled environments with withheld seeds are reserved for future leaderboard evaluation. The release repository includes entrant interfaces for running transition models, policies, and world models against the benchmark locally; these interfaces are not a submission channel.
footer: Data source: aggregate paper results, release 2.2.0.
